Analysis of Deviance for a Generalised Linear Model

Source: R/anova_glm.R
anova_glm.Rd

Fits a generalised linear model of a response on one or more grouping variables in any family, and reports an analysis of deviance table, effect sizes, estimated marginal means and pairwise comparisons.

Usage

anova_glm(
  data,
  response,
  groups,
  family = stats::gaussian(),
  interaction = FALSE,
  type = c("II", "III"),
  test_statistic = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  ci_method = c("profile", "wald"),
  vcov_type = "model",
  adjust = "tukey",
  posthoc = TRUE,
  plots = TRUE,
  weights = NULL,
  verbose = FALSE
)

Arguments

data

A data frame, or anything inheriting from one, such as a data.table or a tibble.

response

Character. Name of the response column. For a binomial or quasi-binomial family it may be 0/1, logical, a proportion (with weights giving the numbers of trials), or a factor or character column with exactly two observed values; the model is then for the second level (in C-locale order for a character column), and $notes names it.

groups

Character vector. One or more grouping columns.

family

A family object, a family function, or the name of one as a character string. Default stats::gaussian().

interaction

FALSE (additive, the default), TRUE (full factorial), or a whole number giving the highest interaction order.

type

Character. "II" (default) or "III" sums of squares. A model with aliased coefficients (an empty cell of the design, or collinear predictors) has no Type III tests; Type II tests are then computed instead, and $notes, the method and the table heading say so.

test_statistic

Character or NULL. One of "LR", "Wald" or "F", passed to Anova. When NULL (the default) it is chosen after fitting: an F test when the fitted model estimates its dispersion – the Gaussian, Gamma, inverse Gaussian, quasi, quasi-Poisson and quasi-binomial families, and MASS::negative.binomial(theta), whose coefficient table also uses t – and a likelihood ratio test when the dispersion is fixed (binomial, Poisson). A quasi family has no likelihood, so "LR" becomes "F" there, with a note, as in anova_count. For any other family that estimates its dispersion, "LR" is car's scaled-deviance chi-square, each change in deviance divided by the estimated dispersion as though it were known; the table heading and $notes say so. "F" on a binomial or Poisson fit is a quasi-likelihood test, since car estimates the dispersion from the Pearson statistic; the method label and $notes say so, and the coefficient table, $emmeans and $posthoc still assume a dispersion of 1.

conf_level

Numeric in (0, 1). Level for every interval returned. Default 0.95.

ci_method

Character. "profile" (default) or "wald" for the coefficient intervals. Both use the reference distribution of the coefficient table's p-values. For a family with a fixed dispersion (binomial, Poisson) the profile interval is stats::confint()'s, which cuts the signed-root deviance profile at normal quantiles. For a family that estimates its dispersion the same profile is cut at qt(., df.residual) instead, the distribution of the t test beside it; for the Gaussian identity model, whose profile is exactly quadratic, it is the Wald t interval confint(lm()), and is computed as such. The p-values in the coefficient table are Wald p-values, so in small or sparse samples a profile interval can exclude the null value while the p-value beside it is above 1 - conf_level, or the reverse; $notes names such rows, and ci_method = "wald" gives intervals that always agree with the p-values. If profiling fails, Wald intervals are used, with a note. A bound the profile cannot reach (as under separation) is NA, also with a note. Profiling refits the model many times for every coefficient, so when ci_method is left at its default and the model has more than 50 coefficients, or the number of coefficients squared times the number of rows exceeds 1e7, Wald intervals are used instead, with a note; give ci_method = "profile" explicitly to profile them anyway. Under separation the interval of a diverged coefficient is found by profiling the likelihood directly when ci_method = "profile", and its ci_method column then says "profile"; ci_method = "wald" keeps the Wald interval, as anova_bin does.

vcov_type

Character. "model" (default) or an HC type ("HC0" to "HC4"), which requires the sandwich package. The robust covariance is used by the coefficient table (with Wald intervals), the marginal means and the comparisons. The omnibus likelihood ratio and F tests are computed from the likelihood and cannot use it; with test_statistic = "Wald" the omnibus test uses it too. $notes says which applies.

adjust

Character. Multiplicity adjustment for the pairwise comparisons, applied by emmeans. One of "tukey", "sidak", "scheffe", "dunnettx", "bonferroni", "holm", "hochberg", "hommel", "BH", "BY", "fdr" or "none". Default "tukey".

posthoc

Logical. Compute pairwise comparisons. There are choose(k, 2) of them, so this is worth turning off when the number of cells is large; $notes records that they were skipped. Default TRUE.

plots

Logical. Build ggplot2 objects. They are returned in $plots, never drawn. Default TRUE.

weights

Optional character. Name of a numeric column of prior weights. Given as a column name rather than a vector so that it is subsetted with the data: a vector supplied by the caller is evaluated against the original frame and silently misaligns as soon as one row is dropped for missing values. Rows with weight zero contribute nothing to the fit; they are dropped before fitting and counted in $n_removed. Whole-number weights (some above 1) are read as frequency weights, each row standing for that many identical observations, in the families where that reading is unambiguous: the Poisson and quasi-Poisson families and MASS::negative.binomial(theta) on counts, and the binomial and quasi-binomial families on a 0/1 response. The robust covariance (vcov_type), the residual degrees of freedom, and so the dispersion, F tests, t intervals, marginal means and BIC, are then those of the data expanded to one row per observation. $model is still the glm as stats::glm() fitted it to the rows, so that anova(), update() and other refits of it stay consistent; its own residual degrees of freedom count rows, and $notes says when that changes what summary(fit$model) would show. In any other family (Gaussian, a linear probability model on a 0/1 response included, Gamma, inverse Gaussian, quasi()) and for other weights (precision weights, or the trials behind a proportion) each row is one unit for the residual degrees of freedom and the robust covariance. The likelihood still multiplies by the weights, as in stats::glm(): a family that estimates its dispersion absorbs their scale (as does MASS::negative.binomial(theta), whose dispersion stats::glm() and summary.glm() estimate), but in a Poisson or binomial fit the likelihood-ratio and Wald statistics and the Pearson dispersion (so the overdispersion check) scale with them, and the intervals narrow as they grow. Unlike anova_count, the dispersion is not computed with the weights rescaled, since it describes the model as weighted; in a Poisson or binomial fit $notes says so when weights that are not whole numbers do not average 1.

verbose

Logical. Emit progress through message. Default FALSE.

Value

An anovakit_fit object, with $family (the family object actually used) and $model_stats (AIC, BIC, the null and residual deviances, and the residual degrees of freedom). For a binomial family with weights that are not all whole numbers, AIC and BIC are NA with a note, as in anova_bin: R's binomial log-likelihood rounds the weights. $anova has the columns term, sum_sq (F tests only), df, statistic and p_value, in that order whatever test_statistic. In an F table of a non-Gaussian family, as car computes it, a term's sum_sq is its change in deviance and the Residuals row holds the Pearson chi-square, from which the dispersion the F statistic divides by is estimated. $assumptions holds coefficients – the coefficient table, with the intervals ci_method selects – and dispersion. $effect_sizes depends on the family:

  • Gaussian: partial eta squared and partial omega squared for each term, from the F table's sums of squares whatever test_statistic is. Partial omega squared is floored at 0, with a note. When the ANOVA table cannot be computed the table is empty and a note says why. (A Type III request on a model with an empty cell is not such a case: Type II tests are computed instead; see type.)

  • Any other family: deviance_explained, 1 - deviance / null deviance, and mcfadden_r2, McFadden's pseudo R squared 1 - logLik(model) / logLik(intercept-only model). McFadden's measure is reported only for the binomial, Poisson and negative binomial families, whose log-likelihoods are probabilities; for a binomial response it is computed from the Bernoulli log-likelihood, so it is the same whether the data are given one row per trial or aggregated as proportions with trial weights (and for a 0/1 response it equals the deviance explained). For the Gamma, inverse Gaussian and quasi families it is NA with a note: a density's log-likelihood changes with the units of the response, and a quasi family has none. The deviance explained is measured against the saturated model, so for binomial data it does depend on the aggregation.

Details

Type III sums of squares. When type = "III" the model is fitted under sum-to-zero contrasts. This is the whole point: setting options(contrasts = ) after a model has been fitted does not change the contrasts stored on it, so car::Anova(type = 3) would silently report simple effects at the reference level under the label "Type III".

Post-hoc. Marginal means and comparisons come from emmeans and are on the response scale. When the grouping variables enter the model additively (the default with more than one), they are reported for each factor on its own, averaged over the others; with an interaction they are made across the cells of the grid. With a log or logit link a comparison is a ratio (of means, or of odds); with any other non-identity link (inverse, probit, square root, ...) it is a difference between the marginal means on the response scale. Families that estimate their dispersion use t with the residual degrees of freedom, as the coefficient table does.

Separation. For binomial, quasi-binomial, Poisson, quasi-Poisson and negative binomial families the fit is checked for groups whose fitted probability is numerically 0 or 1 (or whose fitted rate is numerically 0), where coefficients, Wald tests and comparisons are not identified; $notes says so when it happens.

Exact fits. A family that estimates its dispersion (and any family with test_statistic = "F") divides every test statistic by the residual variation. When the response is constant, or constant within every group, there is none, and the function stops with an error instead of reporting F statistics that are ratios of rounding errors. That includes a frequency table with one row per group, which stands for a response constant within every group. A response with a large level and small but real variation (epoch seconds varying by minutes, say) is not an exact fit: the Gaussian family resolves it. The Poisson, Gamma and negative binomial deviances, however, are computed as differences of nearly equal terms, and on such a level rounding can swamp the change in deviance a test is built on. A likelihood-ratio or F test that rounding could move by more than a fifth of its size or of its size under the null hypothesis (its degrees of freedom for a chi-square, 1 for an F), whichever is larger, is then NA, and one it could move by more than 2% of that gets a note; a negative statistic within its rounding error is shown as 0, with p = 1; $notes says which, and test_statistic = "Wald", which does not use the deviance, can still test them.

Convergence. stats::glm() judges convergence by a change in deviance relative to the deviance plus 0.1, so a fit whose deviance is small because of the units of the response (or the scale of the weights) would stop early. Such a fit is repeated with a convergence tolerance scaled to its deviance, so the results do not depend on the units. A binomial fit with prior weights is glm()'s own fit whenever that reaches the maximum of the likelihood. When it does not (glm()'s default start diverges for a frequency-weighted 0/1 response under a cloglog link), the model is refitted from the overall proportion, to a tight convergence tolerance, and car's refits of reduced models start there too.

For binary responses see anova_bin, and for counts see anova_count: both add family-specific diagnostics and effect sizes that this general wrapper does not.

See also

anova_bin and anova_count, which add family-specific diagnostics and effect sizes.

Examples

set.seed(42)
d <- data.frame(
  A = factor(sample(c("a1", "a2"), 200, replace = TRUE)),
  B = factor(sample(c("b1", "b2"), 200, replace = TRUE))
)
d$y <- 3 + 2 * (d$A == "a2") + (d$B == "b2") +
  4 * (d$A == "a2") * (d$B == "b2") + rnorm(200)

# Type III tests, with the model fitted under sum-to-zero contrasts
fit <- anova_glm(d, "y", c("A", "B"), interaction = TRUE, type = "III")
fit$anova
#>        term   sum_sq  df statistic      p_value
#> 1         A 828.3928   1  924.0123 4.109856e-76
#> 2         B 378.7873   1  422.5099 8.435778e-51
#> 3       A:B 192.5110   1  214.7321 2.549481e-33
#> 4 Residuals 175.7173 196        NA           NA

# The coefficient table, with profile-likelihood intervals by default
fit$assumptions$coefficients
#>          term   estimate         se statistic       p_value distribution
#> 1 (Intercept)  5.4973240 0.06790639  80.95444 1.359261e-152            t
#> 2          A1 -2.0641894 0.06790639 -30.39757  4.109856e-76            t
#> 3          B1 -1.3958190 0.06790639 -20.55505  8.435778e-51            t
#> 4       A1:B1  0.9950827 0.06790639  14.65374  2.549481e-33            t
#>     conf_low conf_high ci_method
#> 1  5.3634030  5.631245   profile
#> 2 -2.1981104 -1.930268   profile
#> 3 -1.5297399 -1.261898   profile
#> 4  0.8611617  1.129004   profile

# A family may be given as a string, as stats::glm() allows. For a binary
# response anova_bin() is usually the better entry point.
d$hit <- rbinom(200, 1, plogis(-0.5 + 1.2 * (d$A == "a2")))
bin <- anova_glm(d, "hit", "A", family = "binomial", plots = FALSE)
bin$anova
#>   term df statistic      p_value
#> 1    A  1  22.84952 1.751931e-06
bin$effect_sizes
#>              measure   estimate
#> 1 deviance_explained 0.08270479
#> 2        mcfadden_r2 0.08270479

# Heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors, which flow through to the
# marginal means and the comparisons
anova_glm(d, "y", "A", vcov_type = "HC3", plots = FALSE)$emmeans
#>    A estimate        se  df conf_low conf_high
#> 1 a1 3.365595 0.1004602 198 3.167486  3.563704
#> 2 a2 7.583053 0.2482866 198 7.093427  8.072679
